newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN BANKS TO PAY 0.06% TAX ON SAVINGS BOOKS.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN BANKS TO PAY 0.06% TAX ON SAVINGS BOOKS.

text.p: The Belgian government has decided banks will have to pay a 0.06 percent tax on the total amount outstanding in savings book accounts, a government source said on Friday.
It added that banks would be allowed to book the tax -- like all indirect taxes -- as a cost. The measures is part of the 1997 budget.
Earlier, another government source said there would be a 0.6 percent tax on savings book turnover.

"It is a tax of 0.06 percent and it will be due on the full amount of savings books accounts as shown on the liabilities side of banks' balance sheets," said the second source, who was involved in drafting the measure.
A Belgian Banking Association report showed that in 1995 the sector had 2,832 billion francs worth of savings books.
At 0.06 percent, this would represent a gross cost of 1.69 billion francs for the sector.
Considering that it would be deducted as a cost and given the 40.2 percent corporate tax rate, the net cost to the sector would just over one billion francs.

The Belgian banking sector made a 49.1 billion franc total net profit in 1994, the most recent date for which sector data are available. In that year, the seven top banks earned a total of 34.4 billion francs.
Savings books are one of Belgium's most popular savings instrument. The first 50,000 francs of interest income earned on them is exempt from withholding tax.
The exemption is limited to one account per person, but many Belgians open several savings book accounts and fail to declare this to the taxman.

The second government source said that measures would be taken to ensure that banks did not pass on the tax to their customers by lowering the interest rates on savings books, but he declined to be more specific.
Belgian media have said that the banking sector would have to contribute five billion francs to the 1997 budget.
This could indicate that a planned 0.3 percent tax on physical delivery of securities -- to be paid by investors -- would cost more than the savings book tax.
